text: Track 6.1 Hello and welcome to the lecture. Do you know what a happy accident is? It's when something happens that isn't planned and turns out to be good for everyone. This happens to scientists quite a lot and they have made some important discoveries as a result. Some of these you may already know about but perhaps you don't know that some were happy accidents. I'd like to start by talking about some surprising numbers. Experts say that between 30 and 50% of the things that scientists discover aren't planned. But the important thing is that the scientist realises it is valuable. So let's have a look at some of these happy accidents. First we'll discuss the discovery of a very important kind of medicine, antibiotics. In 1928, Alexander Fleming was cleaning his laboratory after a holiday when he found a dish of bacteria that he had left out. But he noticed that something had killed the bacteria on it, something he called penicillin. After more research, he found that it could kill other bacteria and didn't hurt animals. Fleming wasn't able to produce large quantities of penicillin, but he published his research in one of the medical journals. Oxford University scientists Howard Flory and Ernst Chain studied penicillin some more and after a lot of research, they developed the first antibiotic in 1942. Next, let's look at the X-ray. In 1895, Wilhelm Konrad-Runtken, a physicist, was doing an experiment with something called a cathode ray tube. A long pipe filled with a special gas, similar to a modern light bulb. When he put electricity into the tube, it lit up. Then he decided to put black paper around it and noticed a green-coloured light coming from a chemical close by. Runtken realized that the cathode ray tube was sending out a new type of light and he discovered this light could go through skin, but not bones or metal. He called the technology X-rays because he didn't really know what they were. Runtken won a Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901 for his discovery. Now I'd like to mention a product I'm sure you all know. Plastic Leo Hendrick Bakeland invented the first kind of plastic in 1907. Bakeland was looking for something to replace the main ingredient in wood polish called shellac, which comes from an insect. People used this to protect wood and other things, but it was very expensive. Bakeland mixed a lot of things together and then heated them up, but he didn't find what he was looking for. Instead, he created something that didn't melt when it got hot or break when someone hit it. Yes, he discovered plastic, a material you can see all around you right now by accident.
